abstract: "Bilateral interbank exposures are rarely published, so studies of contagion and spillovers reconstruct them from each bank's total interbank lending and borrowing. We propose areconstruction that combines a covariate-informed stochastic blockmodel, an amortized recurrent inference network and a differentiable projection onto the published totals and a per-pair regulatory exposure cap, solved by Dykstra's alternating projections. On synthetic blockmodel networks with known ground truth (24 banks, 16 periods, 5 seeds), the reconstruction error is lower than that of the classical RAS method in every seed (paired t-test p = 0.0101), but the latent block labels are not recovered better than a majority guess (p = 0.1136). We then apply the method to a hand-extracted monthly panel of 16 Nepali commercial banks over 133 months. Here the published data, not the model, decide the result. In 43 of 45 months of the clean window, total lending and total borrowing within the 16 banks differ by more than 1% (median relative gap 0.32), so no non-negative matrix can match both totals; the projection returns its least-violation compromise, and its miss tracks the gap (Spearman 0.926). Two model fits whose latent posteriors end at opposite degenerate states give matrices within a relative difference of $1.5\times10^{-5}$. The cap binds for 1.9% of entries in the clean window. We conclude that the method works where its inputs are consistent, and that Nepal's two published marginals do not support a bilateral reconstruction: answering \"who is exposed to whom\" would need bilateral or large-exposure reporting."

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} Interbank networks; network reconstruction; maximum entropy; RAS; stochastic blockmodel; capped matrix balancing; Dykstra's algorithm; emerging markets; Nepal. \vspace{1.5em}

# Introduction {#sec-introduction-network-reconstruction}

Under Section 4 of the Nepal Rastra Bank Act, 2058, a primary mandate of the central bank is to maintain financial sector stability and build public confidence in the banking system. Carrying out this statutory objective requires regulatory tools that are capable of monitoring systemic risk, and if in case of instability surfaces, tools to curtail the contagion [@upper2011simulation]. However, in the current setup the NRB eithr does not publicly acknowledge the types of tools or techniques that it employs to ascertain and contain the systemic risk or at least does to measure the bilateral counterparty exposures. In this context, envisioining and implementing a roubst and transparent framework beyond the traditional regulatroy reporting, particularly that is capable of capturing the bilateral exposure is crucial.

An example of paramount importance is provided by financial systems: information on the interconnections between financial institutions is privacy-protected, dramatically reduc- ing the possibility of correctly estimating crucial systemic properties such as the resilience to the propagation of shocks

are unobserved in Nepal's public monthly returns, evaluating systemic risk requires reconstructing the exposure matrix from aggregate marginal totals...

Statutorily, Section 4 of the Nepal Rastra Bank Act, 2058, mandatess the central bank to maintain finsancial sector stability, sepcially by monitoring interbanking expsoures.

Contagion analysis needs a network, and the network is usually not observed. Central banks and researchers observe each bank's total interbank lending and total interbank borrowing, and must reconstruct the bilateral matrix whose row and column sums these are [@upper2011simulation; @squartini2018reconstruction]. The classical answer spreads the totals as evenly as possible (RAS or maximum entropy, @deming1940least), which is known to produce networks that are too dense and to understate systemic risk where true bilateral data exist for comparison [@mistrulli2011assessing; @anand2018filling].

This paper makes three contributions.

1.  **A capped, covariate-informed reconstruction.** We model the matrix with a stochastic blockmodel whose edge intensities depend on bank covariates, infer it with an amortized recurrent network, and force the output onto the published totals and a per-pair regulatory cap with a differentiable Dykstra projection. The cap is applied to each entry, as an exposure limit is, not to each row total; an earlier capped-Sinkhorn version that capped row totals is documented as a pitfall (Section 3.4).
2.  **A synthetic test with honest scope.** With ground truth available, the method's reconstruction error is lower than RAS's in every seed. Its block labels are not better than a majority guess, so we make no claim about recovering core and periphery.
3.  **A measured data limit on real data.** On Nepal's monthly bulletins, the two published totals do not balance within the observed banks in almost every month. We show what this does to any reconstruction that targets them: the misfit is set by the data, the projection sets the matrix, and the model's latent structure has no detectable effect on the output. For a regulator this is a concrete finding. The imbalance is first of all a sign that the 16 banks are not a closed system — a panel bank can lend to or borrow from institutions outside the panel, so its two totals need not match within the panel even if every figure is correct — and only possibly a sign that the two bulletin lines are defined inconsistently; we cannot separate the two from the published aggregates. Either way a bilateral reconstruction restricted to the panel is not identified from them.

We report the third result as a finding, not a failure. Missing bilateral data is the norm among central banks [@upper2011simulation], and data aggregation problems persist even inside large banks. A method paper that reports what real published data can and cannot support is useful to the many emerging-market regulators who publish similar aggregate returns. A companion paper [@paper2companion] uses the reconstruction as an exposure weight in a study of Nepal's paid-up capital mandate; we do not discuss causal questions here.

Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 sets out the model and the projection. Section 4 describes the data. Section 5 reports the synthetic results and Section 6 the real-data results. Section 7 discusses limitations and Section 8 concludes.



**bilateral exposures and balance sheet data** In abseence of the direct bilateral exposures data, the literature relies on the maximum entropy to reconstruct the interbank networks, spreading the exposures as evenly as possible subject to the constraints (marginals). Originally @sheldon1998interbank borrowed the ME from physics to reconstruct the interbank linkage (@upper2011simulation).

**Matrix balancing and maximum entropy.** Iterative proportional fitting [@deming1940least] rescales a prior matrix until its margins match. Applied to interbank markets [@upper2011simulation], it gives the RAS baseline we use. @squartini2017maximum and @squartini2018reconstruction place these methods in a maximum-entropy ensemble framework. @anand2018filling show that such ensembles spread exposures over too many links relative to observed networks, and @mistrulli2011assessing, with Italian bilateral data, shows how far maximum-entropy contagion estimates can be from those on the observed network.

**Block structure and learned inference.** Interbank markets are often tiered (@craig2014interbank), which motivates a stochastic blockmodel [@holland1983stochastic; @nowicki2001estimation]. Amortized variational inference over interaction graphs [@kipf2018neural] and differentiable relaxations of discrete structure [@mena2018learning] make such models trainable by gradient descent. Our covariate term plays the role of degree correction or fitness, as in @peixoto2020latent.

**Reconstruction as Bayesian inference.** A separate line infers a network from noisy or partial reports of its edges [@guimera2009missing; @martin2016structural; @peixoto2018reconstructing; @peixoto2019reconstruction]. Our setting gives no edge-level signal at all: only row and column sums. These methods are therefore close in spirit  but not drop-in baselines; adapting them to margin-only input is outside our scope.

**Model selection versus recovery.** @vallescatala2018modelselection show that a model's own selection criterion and its link-recovery performance can disagree. Our real-data stability comparison has the same problem, since the model is trained to be smooth (Section 6.5).

# Method {#sec-methodology-exposure-reconstruction}

This section describes formal framework used to  reconstruct sparse, weighted bilateral interbank networks - edge weights represent bilateral lending exposures constrained by publicly available aggregate balance-sheet totals. As noted in @sec-introduction-network-reconstruction, network reconstruction has been widely studied problem using maximum entropy and RAS methods, which tend to produce dense networks that overlook bilateral concentration and misstate contagion risk. At the same time, research on latent network structure and reconstruction from partial/aggregate data shows that recovering latent group structure without direct edge observations introduces identification issues. To fill the gaps, this paper combines a covariate-informed stochastic blockmodel, an amortized recurrent inference network, and a differentiable projection onto the published totals and a per-pair regulatory exposure cap that enables to evaluate reconstruction performance and data-driven identifiability limits. This section is outlined as follows, first, notions used thorughout paper is presented, followed second by a generative model with accouting identities, followed by a constrained projection, inference and training pipeline. 

## Notations {#sec-methodology-notations}


Consider a financial system of  $N$ commercial banks indexed by $i, j \in \{1,\dots,N\}$ that operate over $T$ months indexed by $t \in \{1,\dots,T\}$. From the publicly available balance sheets, for the specific month $t$, one can observe for each bank its total lending ($r_{i,t}$), total borrowing $c_{i,t}$, capital fund $K_{i,t}$, and other covariate vectors $X_{i,t} \in \mathbb{R}^d$. At each month $t$, for banks $i$ and $j$, bilateral exposures are captured by an unobserved matrix $W_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}_{\ge 0}$ with a zero diagonal, where $W_{ij,t}$ denotes bank $i$'s exposure to bank $j$. The diagonal entries of the matrix are zero, i.e., $W_{ii,t} = 0$ for all $i$.


## Generative model and marginal identities{#sec-methodology-generative-model-marginal-identities}

Each bank belongs to an unobserved structural block $z_i \in \{1,\dots,K\}$, drawn from a prior probability vector $\pi$ over $K$ structural roles. That is, specification \ref{eq:latent_z} is part of the generative model that when connected to balancesheet covariates to pairwaise exposure magnitudes and observed balance-sheet totals. 

\begin{flalign}
    z_i &\sim \text{Categorical}(\pi) && \label{eq:latent_z}
\end{flalign}

While $z_i$  (see Equation \ref{eq:latent_z}) captures discrete structural group membership, bank $i$'s observed covariate vector $X_{i,t} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and weight vector $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ generate a strictly positive activity factor $\phi_{i,t} > 0$ at month $t$ as specified in Equation \ref{eq:latent_phi}. This acts as a covariate-based scale term [@peixoto2020latent], allowing balance-sheet covariates to scale expected exposures smoothly alongside block structure.

\begin{flalign}
    \phi_{i,t} &= \exp(w^\top X_{i,t}) && \label{eq:latent_phi} 
\end{flalign}

An ordered pair of banks $(i, j)$ at month $t$, the positive scale parameter $\lambda_{ij,t}$ brings together the structural and covariate channels: it multiplies the block-to-block affinity $\Lambda_{z_i z_j} > 0$ (linking bank $i$'s block $z_i$ to bank $j$'s block $z_j$) by the activity factors $\phi_{i,t}$ of the lender and $\phi_{j,t}$ of the borrower.

\begin{flalign}
    \lambda_{ij,t} &= \Lambda_{z_i z_j}\,\phi_{i,t}\,\phi_{j,t} && \label{eq:expected_flows}
\end{flalign}

Because interbank networks are sparse and skewed—most bank pairs have zero exposure in a given month, while active exposures can be concentrated [@mistrulli2011assessing; @anand2018filling]—we separate link existence from positive magnitude. Using the logistic sigmoid $\sigma(u) = (1 + e^{-u})^{-1}$, the logit $\eta_{ij,t}$ determines the probability $\sigma(-\eta_{ij,t})$ of a zero exposure, while conditional on $\tilde W_{ij,t} > 0$, the raw exposure follows a log-normal distribution with log-scale $\log \lambda_{ij,t}$ (fed from Eq. 3) and log-variance $\sigma^2$, with $\tilde W_{ii,t} = 0$ (no self-lending). In the synthetic generator, $(\pi, w, \Lambda, \eta, \sigma^2)$ generate raw matrices $\tilde W_t$; in the learned model, a neural decoder produces the pairwise parameters.

\begin{flalign}
    \Pr(\tilde W_{ij,t} = 0) &= \sigma(-\eta_{ij,t}), \quad \tilde W_{ij,t} \mid \tilde W_{ij,t} > 0 
    \sim \text{LogNormal}(\log \lambda_{ij,t}, \sigma^2) && \label{eq:zero_inflated_lognormal}
\end{flalign}

These identities link bilateral exposures $W_{ij,t}$ to observed lending totals $r_{i,t}$ (row sums) and borrowing totals $c_{i,t}$ (column sums). Because accounting identities are deterministic balance-sheet definitions rather than noisy observations, we enforce them through projection in Specified as Equation \ref{eq:marginal_sums} rather than placing them inside the likelihood.

\begin{flalign}
    r_{i,t} &= \sum_j W_{ij,t}, \quad c_{j,t} = \sum_i W_{ij,t} && \label{eq:marginal_sums}
\end{flalign}

The zero inflation in (Equation \ref{eq:zero_inflated_lognormal}) reflects that most bank pairs have no exposure. Because (Equation \ref{eq:marginal_sums}) is a deterministic constraint, not a noisy observation, we enforce it in the architecture through a projection (Section 3.3) rather than in the likelihood. $\Lambda$, $w$ and the block-level existence logits are parameters of the synthetic generator only; the trained model replaces (Equation \ref{eq:expected_flows})–(Equation \ref{eq:zero_inflated_lognormal}) with a learned decoder.

Having defined how exposures arise in principle, we now connect raw or proposed matrices to regulatory limits, amortized inference over bank histories, and the training objective. 

## Constrained projection, inference, and training objective {#sec-methodology-constrained-projection-inference-training-objective}

Given a raw matrix $\tilde W_t$, the output is its Euclidean projection onto the intersection of the row-sum set $\mathcal{R}$, the column-sum set $\mathcal{C}$ and the box $\mathcal{B}$:

\begin{flalign}
    W_t = \text{Proj}_{\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{B}}(\tilde W_t), \quad
    \mathcal{B} = \{W : 0 \le W_{ij} \le \kappa K_{i,t}\ \forall j\} &&  \label{eq:capped_projection}
\end{flalign}

The box caps each bilateral exposure at a fraction $\kappa$ of the lender's capital fund, the form of a single-obligor limit. We use $\kappa = 0.05$. We compute (Equation \ref{eq:capped_projection}) with Dykstra's alternating projections [@boyle1986method] (Algorithm \ref{alg:capacitated_projection} )[^1]. Each of the three set projections is closed form: a uniform shift of each row, a uniform shift of each column, and a clip. The iteration converges to the exact projection when the intersection is non-empty, and gradients pass through it by automatic differentiation (the clip has the usual subgradient). When the intersection is empty the iteration returns a least-violation point that keeps the box but misses the margins. We treat that case as a property of the inputs to be reported, not as a solution; on real data it is the usual case.

[^1]: For details refer @boyle1986method and @tibshirani2017dykstra

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
  \caption{Capacitated Projection}
  \label{alg:capacitated_projection}
    \begin{algorithmic}[1]
      \Require $\tilde{W}$ (initial matrix), $r$ (target row sums), $c$ (target column sums), $\text{cap}$ (capacity limits), $n_{\text{iters}}$, $\text{tol}$
      \Ensure $W$ (projected matrix)
      \State $W \leftarrow \tilde{W}$; \quad $I_{\text{row}}, I_{\text{col}}, I_{\text{box}} \leftarrow 0$
      \For{$\text{iter} = 1, \dots, n_{\text{iters}}$}
          \State $W_{\text{prev}} \leftarrow W$
          \State $Y \leftarrow W + I_{\text{row}}; \quad W \leftarrow Y + \frac{r - \text{rowsums}(Y)}{N}; \quad I_{\text{row}} \leftarrow Y - W$
          \State $Y \leftarrow W + I_{\text{col}}; \quad W \leftarrow Y + \frac{c - \text{colsums}(Y)}{N}; \quad I_{\text{col}} \leftarrow Y - W$
          \State $Y \leftarrow W + I_{\text{box}}; \quad W \leftarrow \text{clip}(Y, 0, \text{cap}_i) \text{ for every entry of row } i; \quad I_{\text{box}} \leftarrow Y - W$
          \If{$\|W - W_{\text{prev}}\| < \text{tol}$} 
              \State \textbf{break}
          \EndIf
      \EndFor
      \State \textbf{return} $W$
  \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}


## Recurrent State Encoder and Inference network {#sec-methodology-recurrent-state-encoder-inference-network}

To amortize inference across banks and months without overfitting small panels [@kipf2018neural; @mena2018learning], a GRU updates bank $i$'s hidden state $h_{i,t}$ from its covariates $X_{i,t}$, observed marginals $(r_{i,t}, c_{i,t})$, and prior state $h_{i,t-1}$. Including $(r_{i,t}, c_{i,t})$ alongside $X_{i,t}$ is essential because covariates alone do not reveal latent block assignments $z_i$ under the generative model. From $h_{i,t}$, a small network produces approximate posterior block probabilities $q_\psi(z_i)$, while a pairwise decoder maps bank representations to edge-existence and scale parameters; at evaluation time, we compute point estimates using posterior expectations before applying Algorithm~\ref{alg:capacitated_projection} to eliminate sampling noise. A GRU encodes each bank's history, 

\begin{flalign}
  h_{i,t} = \text{GRU}_\theta([X_{i,t}; r_{i,t}; c_{i,t}], h_{i,t-1})\label{eq:recurrent_state_encoder}
\end{flalign}

The marginals enter the encoder because in (1) (2) the block is drawn independently of the covariates, so covariates alone carry no information about $z$; the marginals do, through $\Lambda$. 

A small network gives: 

\begin{flalign}
  q_\psi(z_i) = \text{softmax}(\text{MLP}_\psi(h_{i,t})) 
\end{flalign}

and a pairwise decoder maps $(h_{i,t}, h_{j,t}, z_i, z_j)$ to $(\eta_{ij,t}, \lambda_{ij,t})$. 

Training samples use the Gumbel-softmax, Gumbel-sigmoid and log-normal reparameterizations; the reported $\hat W_t$ uses posterior means ($q_\psi(z)$, $\sigma(\eta)$ and $\lambda e^{\sigma^2/2}$) before projection, which removes sampling noise from the point estimate. We use a GRU rather than a temporal graph network because the panel is small (16 banks).

## Training objective {#sec-methodology-training-objective}

Finally, we train the model by minimizing $\mathcal{L}$, which combines three terms: a supervised log-likelihood term over true bilateral exposures $W_t^{\text{true}}$ (active only in synthetic experiments where ground truth is observed), a KL divergence term regularizing $q_\psi(z)$ toward prior $p(z)$ (annealed to $\beta_{\max} = 0.15$ over 300 epochs with a $0.05$ free-bits floor), and a temporal smoothness penalty ($\lambda_{\text{smooth}} = 0.05$) on consecutive projected matrices. When bilateral ground truth is unavailable on real balance sheets, the first term vanishes, clarifying why projection constraints and smoothness regularization drive $\hat W_t$—and why model-selection/regularization behavior and link recovery can diverge when edge-level data are absent [@vallescatala2018modelselection; @peixoto2018reconstructing].

\begin{flalign}
    \mathcal{L} &= \underbrace{-\mathbb{E}_q[\log p(W_t^{\text{true}})]}_{\text{synthetic only}} +
    \beta_t\,\text{KL}\big(q_\psi(z)\,\|\,p(z)\big) + \lambda_{\text{smooth}} \sum_t \|W_t -
    W_{t-1}\|_F^2 && \tag{9} \label{eq:loss_function}
\end{flalign}

$\beta_t$ rises linearly to $\beta_{\max} = 0.15$ over 300 epochs, with a free-bits floor of 0.05 per bank and period, and $\lambda_{\text{smooth}} = 0.05$. The code also contains a mutual-information clustering term; a sweep over its weight (Appendix C) found no benefit, and it is set to zero in every reported run.

On real data the first term of (Equation \ref{eq:loss_function}) is identically zero, because no bilateral ground truth exists. The KL term depends only on $q_\psi(z)$ and gives the decoder no gradient. The only term that reaches the decoder is the smoothness penalty on the projected matrices.

# Data {#sec-data}

NRB's monthly *Banking and Financial Statistics* bulletins, published as PDFs. We extract each commercial bank's balance sheet. The two margins are sub-items of the balance sheet: $r_{i,t}$ is `a. Interbank Lending` under `3 SHARE & OTHER INVESTMENT` (assets), and $c_{i,t}$ is `b. Interbank Borrowing` under `2 BORROWINGS` (liabilities). $K_{i,t}$ is `1 CAPITAL FUND`. The five covariates are size (the sum of the ten top-level asset rows), the capital and liquidity ratios, loans over deposits, and NRB borrowing over total borrowing (Appendix B).

**Extraction.** Item numbers drift across eras, lettered sub-items repeat under different parents, early bulletins lack a liabilities total, and rows are interleaved across banks. The extractor keys on normalized label text and parent section, tracks the balance-sheet side per bank, and treats an absent optional row as zero only where it is a component of a sum. An audit of the accounting identities (Paper 2, Section 4.2) finds 96–100% of sheets passing through Falgun 2075 and a sharp collapse from Chaitra 2075; we call the months through Falgun 2075 the clean window. We have not traced the later failures to the PDFs rather than to the extraction.

**Complete-case rule.** We never impute. A bank enters only if every field is present in every month of the modelling window. Missingness here has identifiable causes (an era's numbering, a bank absent from a page) and is not missing completely at random, so imputation would inject bias tied to the failure modes [@little2019statistical]. The rule leaves N = 16 of 33 commercial-bank labels over T = 133 months, Asar 2072 – Shrawan 2083. One calendar month, Kartik 2078, is absent. Section 6.1 reports who is excluded and why.

# Results {#sec-results}

## Synthetic results {#sec-synthetic-results}

The generator (Appendix A, Algorithm 2) draws 24 banks over 16 periods with $K = 2$ blocks, $\Lambda = ([2.5, 0.6], [0.6, 0.2])$ block existence logits $\Lambda = ([2, 0], [0, -2])$ five covariates five covariates with weights $w = (0.05, 0.8, 0.5, -0.3, 0.4)$, $\sigma^2 = 0.15$ and cap 6.0. The ground truth is itself projected through Algorithm 1, so it satisfies the cap the model must satisfy; RAS does not use the cap, an asymmetry that favours our method and that the capped-RAS check in Section 5.4 would isolate. We train for 3,000 epochs on seeds 0–4 and compare (i) the relative Frobenius error of $\hat W_t$ against RAS on the same margins and (ii) block accuracy against the majority-class guess (0.70).

### Reconstruction {.unnumbered}

The model's mean relative error is lower than RAS's in 5/5 seeds (0.430 ± 0.043 vs. 0.566 ± 0.026); a paired t-test across seeds gives p = 0.0101. (With five seeds, Wilcoxon's smallest attainable two-sided p is 0.0625, so we report the t-test.) A capped-RAS baseline — plain Sinkhorn given the same per-pair cap the method uses (Section 5.4) — lets us split that gain into its two sources. Of the 0.136 total improvement over RAS, the cap supplies 0.101 (RAS 0.566 → capped RAS 0.465, paired p = 0.028) and the covariate-informed learned prior supplies the remaining 0.036 (capped RAS 0.465 → model 0.430), the latter small but consistent across all five seeds (paired p = 0.0011). (The two components are computed from the unrounded seed means and so need not equal the differences of the three-digit figures shown here.) About three-quarters of the win is therefore the regulatory cap and one-quarter the learned prior; and that learned-prior quarter is not the block structure. A single-block ($K=1$) ablation leaves reconstruction error statistically unchanged (0.420 vs. 0.430, paired p = 0.36; Section 5.4) — and still below capped RAS — so the gain beyond the cap comes from the covariates, the temporal encoder and the learned decoder, not from the covariate-informed blockmodel.

### Block recovery  {.unnumbered} 

Block accuracy exceeds the majority guess by 0.0781 on average (sd 0.0774), in 3 of 5 seeds (paired t-test p = 0.1136). The margin is smaller than its spread, and two failure modes recur across configurations: collapse to the uniform prior, and confident but wrong assignments. We therefore do not claim that the model identifies core and periphery banks. Table C1 shows that the mutual-information term does not change this at any weight tried.

### What the synthetic win is and is not  {.unnumbered}

The synthetic ground truth comes from the same blockmodel the method assumes, which favours the method. The three checks this invites are now run. The capped-RAS baseline (Section 5.2) attributes about three-quarters of the gain over RAS to the per-pair cap and one-quarter to the learned prior. A single-block ablation ($K=1$) then isolates what the block channel itself contributes: with the number of blocks cut from two to one, reconstruction error is statistically unchanged (0.420 at $K=1$ vs. 0.430 at $K=2$, paired t-test p = 0.36, and still below the 0.465 of capped RAS), while block accuracy collapses mechanically to a single block. Since the block labels are not recovered in the first place (Section 5.3), this says the covariate-informed blockmodel adds nothing to reconstruction beyond the cap, the smoothness prior, the temporal encoder and the learned decoder: the learned-prior quarter of the gain is those components, not the communities. A misspecification check completes the picture. When the generator has no block structure (homogeneous blocks — a pure covariate/degree fitness model), the method still beats RAS in all five seeds, but by far less: model 0.730 vs. RAS 0.759, a mean gap of 0.029 against the 0.136 it has on block-structured data. Block accuracy sits exactly at the trivial majority guess (0.524 vs. 0.522, gap 0.002), so the model does not invent communities that are not there. Imposing the blockmodel therefore does not hurt under misspecification: the reconstruction advantage shrinks toward the cap-only margin and the latent structure stays inert, consistent with Sections 5.2–5.3.

A persistence baseline is reported on the real panel in Section 6.5; on the synthetic panel it is uninformative, because the generator redraws blocks and covariates independently each period, so consecutive $W_t$ carry no temporal dependence for a persistence rule to exploit.

## Real-data results

The 16 banks are ADBNL, EBL, Global, HBL, Kumari, Laxmi, MBL, NABIL, NBL, NIC, NMB, NSBI, Prime, RBB, SBL and SCBNL. Three facts limit what the panel represents. - **It is a closed system.** Exposures to the other commercial banks, development banks, NRB and foreign banks are outside the matrix. - **The discard is not size-neutral.** Excluded banks are smaller (pre-window size medians 64,910 NPR mn included vs. 44,510 excluded; Mann–Whitney p = 0.005). - **Some exclusions come from later months.** Over the clean window alone (45 months), 21 labels are complete. BOK (first incomplete month Poush 2079), NCC (Poush 2079), NIBL (Magh 2079), Sunrise (Asar 2080) and Mega (Asar 2076) are dropped only because the filter runs over all 133 months. Why these series stop has not been verified. - **Some exclusions may be relabels.** Citizens→Citizen, NBB→NBBL, PRABHU→Prabhu and Civil→CBL each switch label at Poush/Magh 2075 with no overlap and size and capital ratios of 0.969–1.042 across the switch. Each half fails the complete-case rule. We have not checked these against NRB records, so "33" counts labels; there are at most 29 distinct banks if all four are relabels.

### The published margins do not balance {.unnumbered}

In the clean window (45 months, 720 bank-months), lending is zero in 398 bank-months and borrowing in 465. Within the 16 banks, total lending and total borrowing differ by more than 1% in 43 of 45 months and by more than 10% in 37; the median relative gap is 0.32 and the maximum 0.93 (Mangsir 2072: lending NPR 10,322 mn vs. borrowing NPR 743 mn). In 16 bank-months one bank lends more than all the others borrow, and in 2 one bank borrows more than all the others lend. A non-negative matrix with zero diagonal must have equal totals and must not let one row exceed the other columns' total, so in 43 of 45 months no such matrix matches both margins, before the cap is considered.

Within-panel imbalance is expected whenever the 16 banks are not a closed system: a panel bank's lending total counts loans to banks outside the panel, whose matching borrowing is not in the panel's column totals, so the two panel totals need not be equal even if every figure is correct. This is the leading explanation. A difference in how the two bulletin lines are defined would also produce it, and we cannot say from the published aggregates how much of the gap is open-system leakage and how much, if any, is definitional; we have not checked the line definitions with NRB.

### What the projection does with infeasible margins {.unnumbered}

With an empty intersection, Algorithm 1 returns its least-violation point, and that is the $\hat W_t$ we report. Its worst monthly miss tracks the gap (Spearman 0.93): the median worst miss is NPR 200.8 mn in the 43 infeasible months and 22.28 mn in the other 2. The largest misses are NPR 2,311 mn on lending and 437.8 mn on borrowing. The projection does not keep zeros: $\hat W_t$ assigns more than NPR 1 mn of borrowing to all 465 bank-months that report none (16 of 16 banks; median 100.9, maximum 437.8) and more than NPR 1 mn of lending to 249 of the 398 that report none (13 banks; median 27.1, maximum 833.4).

RAS fits the same margins differently. It rescales entries, so it keeps every zero, matches lending to within NPR 41 mn, and leaves the whole gap on borrowing (deviations up to NPR 8,290 mn). Both methods' worst misses track the gap (Spearman 0.93 for each, Paper 2 Section 8). The size of the misfit is therefore a property of the published data; how it is split is a property of each method. The two networks are not independent estimates: they share their targets, and a downstream exposure measure built from them correlates 0.968 over the companion paper's post-mandate cells.

The cap rarely binds: 7.0% of entries over all 133 months and 1.9% in the clean window ($\kappa = 0.05$). On real data the cap adds little information beyond the margins; its role rests on the synthetic results.

### The model's latent structure does not reach the output {.unnumbered}

We ran two fits that differ only in the KL weight. With $\beta_{\max} = 0.15$ every bank's posterior is near uniform (about 0.45/0.55); with $\beta_{\max} = 0$ the KL term saturates at 0.691 ($\approx \ln 2$) and all 16 banks sit at $\ge 0.999$ on the same block. The two posteriors are at opposite degenerate ends, yet the two $\hat W_t$ series differ by a relative Frobenius difference of $1.5\times10^{-5}$ (maximum absolute difference NPR 0.18 mn). On a matched synthetic pair, where the reconstruction term is active, a much smaller posterior change (mean absolute difference 0.044) moves $\hat W_t$ by a relative difference of 0.285.

This follows from Section 3.6. Without ground truth, no loss term rewards any particular matrix among those near the margins, and the decoder receives gradient only through the smoothness penalty. On real data, $\hat W_t$ is the projection of a smooth, nearly arbitrary raw matrix onto inconsistent margins, and the blockmodel and covariates do not detectably shape it.

### Temporal stability {.unnumbered}

$\hat W_t$ changes less from month to month than RAS: the mean month-to-month change of $\hat W_t$ is 1.16 against RAS's 2.32 (lower is more stable; seed 0, 16 banks over 133 months). But this edge is not evidence that the model recovers stable structure. A persistence baseline makes the point: carrying last month's reconstruction forward and re-imposing the current month's margins and cap through Algorithm 1 already gives a month-to-month change of 1.11 — essentially the model's own 1.16. The model departs from that carried-forward matrix by only 13%, so it adds almost nothing beyond persistence plus marginal-fitting. The gap to RAS therefore reflects that RAS over-reacts to month-to-month noise in the published margins, not that the model's smoothness prior or latent structure contributes stability of its own [@vallescatala2018modelselection]. This is consistent with Section 6.4: on real data the decoder receives gradient only through the smoothness penalty.

# Discussion and limitations

**What the method offers.** Where margins are consistent, the capped projection gives the nearest matrix that matches the totals and respects a per-counterparty limit, and the synthetic results show that the learned prior improves on RAS when there is a signal to learn. The projection is a standalone, differentiable layer that other reconstruction models can use.

**What Nepal's bulletins allow.** Three findings bound any reconstruction from these data, not only ours. First, the two published lending and borrowing totals do not balance within the observed banks in 43 of 45 clean months — most likely because the panel is not a closed system, possibly also because the two lines are defined differently — so an exact bilateral reconstruction restricted to the panel does not exist and every method must choose where to put the misfit. Second, most bank-months report zero, so the margins carry little information about who trades with whom. Third, without bilateral ground truth, nothing in the data selects one matrix over another near the margins; our model's latent structure has no detectable effect on its output. For NRB, the practical implication is that bilateral or large-exposure reporting, even at low frequency, would be needed to make interbank exposure maps informative; reconciling the definitions of the two published interbank lines would be a cheapder first step.

**Limitations.** - *Ground truth.* All accuracy evidence is synthetic and from the assumed model class. The capped-RAS decomposition (Section 5.2), the single-block ($K=1$) ablation and the non-SBM misspecification check (Section 5.4), and the real-data persistence baseline (Section 6.5) are all now run. Even where bilateral data exist, reconstructions differ substantially from them [@mistrulli2011assessing]. - *Block identity.* Not recovered on synthetic data and not identifiable on real data; we make no claim about it. - *Sample.* A closed system of 16 larger banks; the complete-case rule over the full span drops five banks that are complete in the clean window, and four possible relabels are unresolved. - *Training window.* The model is trained on all 133 months, including bulletins whose line items fail the accounting identities from Chaitra 2075. Each month's matrix is fitted to that month's margins, but the smoothness penalty links Falgun 2075 to Chaitra 2075. A run on the clean window only would remove this and could raise N to 21; a larger panel would also show how much of the Section 6.2 imbalance is open-system leakage rather than definitional. It is not done. - *Single seed on real data.* Seed sensitivity of the real-data $\hat W_t$ is not measured, and reconstruction uncertainty is not propagated to downstream uses. - *Model size.* The reconstruction network has 2,133 trainable parameters (GRU encoder 1,200; block-posterior MLP 306; pairwise decoder 626; one scalar dispersion), fixed entirely by the architecture ($d=5$ covariates, hidden width 16, $K=2$ blocks) and independent of panel size — the same network serves the synthetic ($N=24$, $T=16$) and real ($N=16$, $T=133$) panels. On the real panel this is comparable to $N \times T = 2{,}128$ and smaller than the $2NT = 4{,}256$ observed marginals, and about two orders of magnitude below the supervised synthetic target entries used in training. The network is therefore under- rather than over-parameterized: amortization replaces the $N(N-1)T \approx 3.2 \times 10^4$ per-period latent unknowns a non-amortized reconstruction would carry with $\approx 2.1 \times 10^3$ shared weights, a $>10\times$ reduction in effective degrees of freedom. The binding constraint is not model capacity but identifiability of the bilateral matrix from its margins (Section 6.4), which no parameter budget resolves.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusions}

We give a differentiable, capped projection for interbank reconstruction and embed it in a covariate-informed blockmodel. On synthetic data the combination reconstructs better than RAS but does not recover blocks. On Nepal's bulletins the published lending and borrowing totals do not balance within the observed banks, the projection's misfit tracks that imbalance, and the model's latent structure leaves the output unchanged. The result is a measured data limit: the published marginals cannot say who is exposed to whom, and we state what reporting would be needed to change that.

## Appendix A — Algorithms 2 and 3  {.unnumbered} 

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{Sample Synthetic Network}
  \begin{algorithmic}[1]
  \Require $N, K, \pi, \Lambda, H, w, \sigma^2, X, \kappa, K_{\text{cap}}$
  \Ensure $W_{\text{true}}, \text{rowsums}(W_{\text{true}}), \text{colsums}(W_{\text{true}})$
  \For{$i = 1, \dots, N$}
      \State $z_i \sim \text{Categorical}(\pi); \quad \phi_i \leftarrow \exp(w^\top X_i)$
  \EndFor
  \For{$i \neq j$}
      \State $\lambda_{ij} \leftarrow \Lambda_{z_i, z_j} \, \phi_i \, \phi_j$
      \State $e_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\sigma(H_{z_i, z_j}))$
      \State $\tilde{W}_{ij} \leftarrow e_{ij} \cdot \text{LogNormal}(\log \lambda_{ij}, \sigma^2)$
  \EndFor
  \State $W_{\text{true}} \leftarrow \text{CapacitatedProjection}\big(\tilde{W}, \text{rowsums}(\tilde{W}), \text{colsums}(\tilde{W}), \kappa \cdot K_{\text{cap}}\big)$
  \State \textbf{return} $W_{\text{true}}, \text{rowsums}(W_{\text{true}}), \text{colsums}(W_{\text{true}})$
  \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{Training Step}
  \begin{algorithmic}[1]
  \Require Batch $\{X_t, r_t, c_t, K_t\}$, optional $W_{\text{true}, t}$
  \For{$t$ in temporal order}
      \State $h_{i,t} \leftarrow \text{GRU}\left([X_{i,t}; r_{i,t}; c_{i,t}], \, h_{i,t-1}\right)$
      \State $q_i \leftarrow \text{softmax}\big(\text{MLP}(h_{i,t})\big)$
      \State $z_i \leftarrow \text{GumbelSoftmax}(q_i)$
      \State $(\eta_{ij,t}, \lambda_{ij,t}) \leftarrow \text{Decoder}(h_{i,t}, h_{j,t}, z_i, z_j)$
      \State $\tilde{W}_{ij,t} \leftarrow \text{GumbelSigmoid}(\eta_{ij,t}) \cdot \text{LogNormal}(\log \lambda_{ij,t}, \sigma^2)$
      \State $W_t \leftarrow \text{CapacitatedProjection}(\tilde{W}_t, r_t, c_t, \kappa \cdot K_t)$
      \If{$W_{\text{true}, t}$ is given}
          \State $L_{\text{recon}, t} \leftarrow -\log p(W_{\text{true}, t} \mid \lambda_t, \eta_t, \sigma^2)$
      \Else
          \State $L_{\text{recon}, t} \leftarrow 0$
      \EndIf
      \State $L_{\text{KL}, t} \leftarrow \text{KL}\big(q(z_t) \,\|\, p(z)\big)$
  \EndFor
  \State $L \leftarrow \sum_t \left(L_{\text{recon}, t} + \beta \cdot L_{\text{KL}, t}\right) + \lambda_{\text{smooth}} \sum_t \|W_t - W_{t-1}\|_F^2$
  \State backpropagate through Algorithm 1; optimizer step
  \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
